catalog_quote: Distinctive linguistic traits include the presence of distinctive lexical tone, SOV constituent order, and ergativity. [p. 323] ... The investigation of Suansu prosody is in the works: word boundaries reflect native speakers’ intuitions. The description of Suansu tone is in progress, hence tone is not marked on the examples. Tonal distinctions play no role in the expression of phasal polarity. [p. 325 fn. 7] ... While the investigation of Suansu morphophonology is in the works, initial observations regarding prosodic cues (e.g., the presence of stress domain spanning the entire verb complex) indicate a certain degree of phonological boundedness of these markers to the respective host. [p. 332] || Ivani & Tulchynska 2025: 32: Lexical units are identified based on phonological independence, which is determined by the presence of primary stress. || Joessing 2025: 4 (summarising Ivani 2023): Ivani (2023) finds that Suansu exhibits a sesquisyllabic structure, aligning it with many of its neighbors. This finding is relevant to the present study as it means the language contains minor syllables, which are phonetically reduced, lack stress and tone contrasts, and typically feature a highly reduced vowel. Examples of this structure in Suansu include әke ‘go up’, and məlaj ‘needle’.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Suansu is a tone language (lexical tone; three tones per Ivani 2022: 69, a two-way contour contrast in Joessing's 2025 instrumental BA study). Stress is mentioned only as a word-delimiting property: each phonological word carries one primary stress (Ivani & Tulchynska 2025: 32, 'Lexical units are identified based on phonological independence, which is determined by the presence of primary stress'), and the stress domain spans the whole verb complex (verb plus bound formatives). No published source states the position of stress. The only positional hint is second-hand: minor syllables of sesquisyllables 'lack stress and tone contrasts' (Joessing 2025: 4, citing Ivani 2023), which implies prominence on the major (final) syllable of sesquisyllabic words.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in any opened source.
new_statements.exceptions: None; authors state prosody, tone and morphophonology descriptions are still in progress.
new_statements.domain_note: Word / verb-complex level: stress diagnoses phonological wordhood (whitespace in the UD treebank), stress domain = entire verb complex including suffixed negator, completive and focus formatives. Tone is lexical at the word level; not marked in examples. Data from fieldwork with Suansu speakers in Pune and Ukhrul, 2017-2022.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe the same variety: Suansu of Ukhrul district, Manipur (Glottolog suan1234, no ISO code; UD uses the Tangkhul code [nmf] with treebank name 'Naga-Suansu'). Ivani's 2024 Himalayan Linguistics field reports on Kongai and Challow (same district, same author) concern different languages and were not used.

sources.note: p.4 (sec. 2.3, summarising Ivani 2023): Suansu is sesquisyllabic; 'minor syllables, which are phonetically reduced, lack stress and tone contrasts, and typically feature a highly reduced vowel', e.g. əke 'go up', məlaj 'needle'; 'Suansu has lexical tone at the word level' with minimal pair θʌ́ 'feces' vs θʌ̀ 'face'. Instrumental sec. 4.4/5.3: two-way tone contrast (level/rising vs falling) carried by the major syllable. No positive stress-position rule.
